label: R11
title: Recitation 11: Case Study, TAVR or SAVR?
brief: Recitation 11 assembles the course's tools into one prescriptive pipeline for a real clinical choice: SAVR (open-heart surgery) or TAVR (catheter) for patients with severe aortic stenosis at low to intermediate surgical risk, minimizing 3-year mortality. Pre-procedure tabular data, clinical notes and CT scans are embedded per modality with frozen encoders (HAIM), then patients are matched 1:1 within five STS-risk buckets by solving an assignment problem (R.O.A.D.), keeping 326 of 597. Doubly robust, cross-fitted rewards from random survival forests estimate each patient's mortality under both procedures. A prescriptive neural network with a softmax policy minimizes expected estimated mortality, with a penalty $\lambda$ against changing survivors' treatments tuned by the policy's sensitivity and specificity; a locally run LLM only explains its recommendation. Out of sample, estimated mortality falls 34% at Hartford and 45% at St. Vincent's, but the intervals are wide and include zero, and unobserved confounding remains.
kp: Choice: SAVR (open-heart) vs TAVR (catheter) for low-to-intermediate-risk severe aortic stenosis; minimize 3-year all-cause mortality.
Data: Hartford 597 training / 138 validation; St. Vincent's 169 external (about 89% TAVR); pre-procedure tabular, notes, CT.
Embed each modality (tabular as recorded, ClinicalBERT, GigaHeart) and concatenate; encoders frozen (~110M parameters vs 597 patients).
Match 1:1 within five STS buckets on standardized age, sex, BMI via an assignment problem: 326 kept, 271 dropped; observed covariates only.
Rewards $\Gamma_{it}$ = estimated P(death within 3 years) under each procedure: doubly robust, random survival forests, 5-fold cross-fitted.
DR: $f_t(x_i)+\frac{1\{t_i=t\}}{p_t(x_i)}(y_i-f_t(x_i))$, correct if either model is; matching first keeps inverse weights near 2 instead of 7-9.
Policy: PNN with a softmax over procedures, loss = expected estimated mortality, trained by SGD; policy-tree splits on embeddings are unreadable.
Penalty $\lambda$ (cross-entropy toward survivors' treatments) = 'don't change what worked', the policy-side analogue of ROAD I's $\omega$; $\lambda=1$ chosen on Hartford validation.
Specificity = survivors whose treatment is kept; sensitivity = deaths whose treatment is changed; larger $\lambda$ trades sensitivity for specificity.
Results: est. mortality 7.0% to 4.7% (Hartford), 11.5% to 6.4% (St. Vincent's), CIs include zero; the LLM (local Qwen3-14B) only explains.

topics.x: Severe aortic stenosis (3.4% of adults over 75) is treated by replacing the valve, either by open-heart surgery (SAVR) or by catheter (TAVR); at low to intermediate surgical risk the choice is made case by case. The goal is the procedure that minimizes this patient's 3-year mortality, learned from 597 Hartford training patients, with Hartford validation (138) and St. Vincent's (169) held out. The solution chains five steps from the course: embed, match, estimate counterfactuals, learn a policy, explain.

Following HAIM (Lecture 17), each modality gets its own embedding: tabular features as recorded, notes through ClinicalBERT, CT scans through GigaHeart. The three are concatenated into $x_i$, the input to steps 2-4. The encoders stay frozen because ClinicalBERT alone has about 110 million parameters against 597 patients with few deaths.

Treatment depends on risk: TAVR goes mostly to high-STS patients and SAVR to low-STS ones. Patients are bucketed into five STS-score groups and matched 1:1 within each bucket on standardized age, sex and BMI by solving an assignment problem. This keeps 326 of 597 patients and balances observed covariates only.

Each patient has one observed outcome, so rewards $\Gamma_{iS},\Gamma_{iT}$ (estimated probability of death within 3 years) fill in both procedures. The doubly robust estimator combines a random-survival-forest outcome model and a propensity model and is correct if either is; cross-fitting ensures no patient's reward comes from a model trained on that patient. Matching first keeps propensities near 1/2, so inverse weights stay near 2.

topics.n: Prescriptive network and the lambda penalty
topics.x: Policy trees on embeddings give meaningless splits, so a prescriptive neural network (Lecture 19) outputs softmax probabilities over SAVR/TAVR and minimizes expected estimated mortality by SGD. A cross-entropy penalty $\lambda$ toward the treatment survivors received encodes 'don't change treatments that already worked', analogous to ROAD I's weight $\omega$. $\lambda$ is tuned on Hartford validation by the policy's sensitivity and specificity; $\lambda=1$ was selected.

An LLM is not trained on this outcome, is poorly calibrated and would face long, mostly irrelevant records, so it only explains the PNN's choice, as in xHAIM (Lecture 18). Qwen3-14B runs inside the hospital because records cannot leave. The prompt has it list and judge the documented findings, keeping those that favor the other procedure, before it reads the recommendation.

Reward models and the PNN are fit on Hartford training and frozen; the policy is scored on held-out patients as the mean reward of its chosen treatments. Estimated 3-year mortality drops 34% at Hartford and 45% at St. Vincent's, with specificity about 0.8 and sensitivity 0.5, and blinded cardiologists judge 85% and 93% of choices compatible. Confidence intervals are wide and include zero; unobserved confounding, the small sample and the single outcome remain limitations, and a pilot at Hartford is next.

cards.f: What decision does the TAVR-or-SAVR case study make, and for whom?
cards.b: For patients with severe aortic stenosis at low to intermediate surgical risk, choose SAVR (open-heart surgery) or TAVR (catheter valve replacement) to minimize that patient's 3-year mortality.
cards.x: Replacement itself is not in question: untreated, 50.7% died within a year (PARTNER cohort B).

cards.f: Name the five steps of the pipeline and the lecture each comes from.
cards.b: 1 Embed tabular, notes, CT (L17 HAIM); 2 match within risk buckets (L13-14 R.O.A.D.); 3 doubly robust counterfactuals (L11 reward estimation); 4 policy via prescriptive network (L11 policy trees, L19 prescriptive DL); 5 grounded LLM explanation (L18 xHAIM).
cards.x: Embed, match, reward, prescribe, explain: each step feeds the next.

cards.f: How is the patient representation $x_i$ built?
cards.b: One embedding per modality: tabular features (history, echo, CT measurements) as recorded, clinical notes via ClinicalBERT, CT scans via GigaHeart. Concatenate: $x_i=[E_{tab}(i),E_{notes}(i),E_{img}(i)]$, the input to steps 2-4.
cards.x: Trap: the encoders are not fine-tuned here; 597 patients with few deaths cannot train ~110M ClinicalBERT parameters.

cards.f: What are the three steps of prognostic matching in this study?
cards.b: 1 Score each patient's surgical risk with the STS score (ROAD I instead fits a model $g$); 2 cut five STS buckets; 3 match 1:1 within each bucket on age, sex and body mass index.
cards.x: Bucketing balances risk; the within-bucket match balances demographics.

cards.f: Write the matching problem for STS bucket $k$.
cards.b: $\min_z \sum_{i\in S^{min}_k}\sum_{j\in S^{max}_k} z_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2$ s.t. $\sum_{j\in S^{max}_k} z_{ij}=1\ \forall i\in S^{min}_k$, $\sum_{i\in S^{min}_k} z_{ij}\le 1\ \forall j\in S^{max}_k$, $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$; $x$ = standardized (age, sex, BMI).
cards.x: Equality: every smaller-arm patient gets a partner. At most 1: no larger-arm partner is reused.

cards.f: What does matching cost, and what can it not fix?
cards.b: 271 of 597 training patients are dropped (326 kept, 163 per arm). It balances observed covariates only: unrecorded frailty can still differ between arms (Lecture 14's $U$).
cards.x: Matching is done on the training set only.

cards.f: Why does the method need rewards $\Gamma_{it}$ at all?
cards.b: Each patient has one observed outcome, under the procedure received, but scoring a policy needs mortality under both. $\Gamma_{iS},\Gamma_{iT}$ fill this in; $f_t$ is a random survival forest and $\Gamma_{it}$ is the probability of death within 3 years.
cards.x: Reward estimation (Lecture 11) turns a missing-data problem into a full table.

cards.f: Give the direct, inverse-propensity and doubly robust rewards and each one's weakness.
cards.b: DM: $\Gamma_{it}=f_t(x_i)$, biased if $f_t$ is wrong. IPW: $\Gamma_{it}=\frac{1\{t_i=t\}}{p_t(x_i)}y_i$, high variance when $p_t(x_i)$ is small. DR: $\Gamma_{it}=f_t(x_i)+\frac{1\{t_i=t\}}{p_t(x_i)}(y_i-f_t(x_i))$, correct if either model is.
cards.x: DR = direct method plus an inverse-propensity-weighted residual on the observed arm only.

cards.f: What is cross-fitting and why is it used?
cards.b: Split into 5 folds; fit $f_t$ and $p_t$ on four folds, compute $\Gamma_{it}$ on the fifth, rotate. No patient's reward comes from a model trained on that patient.

Before matching, propensities are extreme: SAVR is 13 of 121 in the riskiest bucket (weight about 9), TAVR 17 of 119 in the safest (about 7). After matching each arm is half of every bucket, so weights are about 2.
cards.x: Propensities near 0 or 1 give unstable weights (Lecture 14).

cards.f: Why a prescriptive neural network rather than an optimal policy tree?
cards.b: The objective is $\min_\pi\sum_i\sum_{t\in\{S,T\}}1\{\pi(x_i)=t\}\Gamma_{it}$. A tree on embeddings would split on things like $E_{notes}(i)_{412}\le 0.3$, meaningless to a clinician, so a PNN is trained and explained afterwards (mirrored tree on tabular data, or an LLM).
cards.x: Interpretability moves from the model to the explanation step.

cards.f: Describe the PNN's architecture and training loss.
cards.b: $x_i$ to 64 ReLU to 32 ReLU to scores $s_S,s_T$; softmax $p_\theta(t\mid x_i)=e^{s_t}/(e^{s_S}+e^{s_T})$. Loss $\frac1N\sum_i\sum_t p_\theta(t\mid x_i)\Gamma_{it}$; prescribe the larger $p_\theta$.
cards.x: Softmax replaces the hard rule $1\{s_T>s_S\}$ so the loss is differentiable and trainable by SGD.

cards.f: How is 'don't change treatments that already worked' built into the loss?
cards.b: Add $\lambda\left(-\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i\in G}\log p_\theta(t_i\mid x_i)\right)$: cross-entropy toward the treatment given, over survivors $G$. $\lambda=0$: PNN alone; large $\lambda$: copy the heart team.
cards.x: Policy-side analogue of ROAD I's weight $\omega$, which sits in the counterfactual model instead.

cards.f: Define a policy's sensitivity and specificity in this study.
cards.b: Compare the policy with the treatment given, split by outcome. Specificity: survivors whose treatment is kept. Sensitivity: deaths whose treatment is changed. Never switch: specificity 1, sensitivity 0; always switch: 0 and 1.
cards.x: Larger $\lambda$ raises specificity and lowers sensitivity; $\lambda=1$ was chosen on Hartford validation.

cards.f: Why does an LLM explain the recommendation rather than make it?
cards.b: It was not trained on this outcome and is poorly calibrated; patient records are long and mostly irrelevant; and records cannot leave the hospital, so the LLM (Qwen3-14B) runs locally. It only explains the PNN's recommendation, as in xHAIM.
cards.x: The model decides; the LLM grounds the decision in the patient's record.

cards.f: How is the policy evaluated out of sample?
cards.b: Fit the reward models and PNN on Hartford training and freeze them. For held-out patients, compute $\Gamma_{it}$ from the frozen reward models and their own outcomes, then $\hat V(\pi)=\frac1n\sum_i\Gamma_{i,\pi(x_i)}$.
cards.x: Lecture 11 refits reward models on the test set; St. Vincent's (19 SAVR patients, 14 deaths) is too small for that.

quiz.q: In the TAVR-or-SAVR study, which outcome does the learned policy try to minimize?
o: Death from any cause within 3 years of the procedure
The STS score's predicted surgical mortality
Death within 1 year, as reported for PARTNER cohort B
Nonfatal complications and later valve wear
quiz.e: The outcome recorded for every cohort is death from any cause within 3 years, and the stated goal is minimizing 3-year mortality. The STS score is a pre-procedure risk score used for bucketing, and nonfatal complications are explicitly not counted (a listed limitation).

quiz.q: Why are the ClinicalBERT and GigaHeart encoders kept frozen instead of fine-tuned?
o: ClinicalBERT alone has about 110 million parameters, and there are only 597 training patients with few deaths
Doubly robust rewards require fixed, non-learned features
Fine-tuning would break the 1:1 matching within STS buckets
The local LLM can only read frozen embeddings
quiz.e: Fine-tuning backpropagates through ~110M parameters, which 597 patients with few deaths cannot support (xHAIM had tens of thousands of ICU stays). Nothing in the DR estimator or the matching needs frozen features; matching uses age, sex and BMI.

quiz.q: In the matching problem for STS bucket $k$, which constraint guarantees that every patient in the smaller arm is matched?
o: $\sum_{j\in S^{max}_k} z_{ij}=1$ for all $i\in S^{min}_k$
$\sum_{i\in S^{min}_k} z_{ij}\le 1$ for all $j\in S^{max}_k$
$\sum_{i}\sum_{j} z_{ij}=|S^{max}_k|$
$z_{ij}\ge 0$ for all $i,j$
quiz.e: Summing over partners $j$ for each smaller-arm patient and setting it to 1 forces exactly one match each. The $\le 1$ constraint over $i$ only stops a larger-arm patient from being reused; demanding $|S^{max}_k|$ matches is infeasible when the arms differ in size.

quiz.q: Before matching, the 1.38-1.92% STS bucket has 45 SAVR and 74 TAVR patients. After 1:1 matching within the bucket, how many patients from it remain?
quiz.e: Every patient in the smaller arm (45 SAVR) gets one distinct TAVR partner: 45 pairs = 90 patients, and 29 TAVR patients are dropped (the after-matching panel shows 45 and 45). 45 counts one arm only; 119 is the bucket before matching.

quiz.q: Patient $i$ received TAVR and died within 3 years ($y_i=1$). The cross-fitted models give $f_T(x_i)=0.10$ and $p_T(x_i)=0.4$. What is the doubly robust reward $\Gamma_{iT}$?
quiz.e: $\Gamma_{iT}=f_T+\frac{1}{p_T}(y_i-f_T)=0.10+2.5\times0.90=2.35$. 0.10 is the direct method and 2.50 the IPW reward $y_i/p_T$; 0.90 is the residual alone. An individual DR reward can exceed 1; the estimator is correct if either model is.

quiz.q: For the same TAVR patient, $f_S(x_i)=0.15$ and $p_S(x_i)=0.6$. What is the doubly robust reward $\Gamma_{iS}$?
quiz.e: The indicator $1\{t_i=S\}=0$, so the correction term vanishes and $\Gamma_{iS}=f_S(x_i)=0.15$. 0 is what IPW gives for the unobserved arm; 1.57 wrongly applies the correction $0.15+(1-0.15)/0.6$ to a procedure the patient never had.

quiz.q: With 5-fold cross-fitting, how is $\Gamma_{it}$ computed for a patient in fold 3?
o: From $f_t$ and $p_t$ fit on folds 1, 2, 4 and 5
From $f_t$ and $p_t$ fit on all five folds
From $f_t$ and $p_t$ fit on fold 3 alone
By averaging the predictions of all five rounds' models
quiz.e: Each round fits $f_t$ and $p_t$ on four folds and computes rewards on the held-out fifth, so no reward comes from a model trained on that patient. Fitting on all folds, or averaging all five rounds (one of which trained on fold 3), breaks that rule.

quiz.q: In the riskiest STS bucket before matching, 13 of 121 patients received SAVR. Using a bucket-level propensity, what inverse-propensity weight $1/p_S$ does a SAVR patient there get, and roughly what is it after matching?
o: About 9 before, about 2 after
About 1.1 before, about 2 after
About 0.11 before, 0.5 after
About 9 before, 1 after
quiz.e: $p_S\approx13/121\approx0.107$, so $1/p_S\approx9.3$; after 1:1 matching each arm is half the bucket, $p\approx0.5$, weight about 2. 1.1 is the majority TAVR arm's weight ($121/108$); 0.11 and 0.5 are propensities, not weights.

quiz.q: A PNN gives patient $i$ scores $s_S=0$ and $s_T=\ln 3$, with rewards $\Gamma_{iS}=0.20$ and $\Gamma_{iT}=0.08$. What is this patient's term in the PNN loss (no penalty)?
quiz.e: $p_\theta(T\mid x_i)=e^{\ln 3}/(1+e^{\ln 3})=0.75$, so the term is $0.25\cdot0.20+0.75\cdot0.08=0.05+0.06=0.11$. 0.08 is the hard policy's value (prescribe TAVR); 0.17 swaps the probabilities; 0.14 is the unweighted mean of the two rewards.

quiz.q: In the loss $\frac1N\sum_i\sum_t p_\theta(t\mid x_i)\Gamma_{it}+\lambda\left(-\frac{1}{|G|}\sum_{i\in G}\log p_\theta(t_i\mid x_i)\right)$, what happens as $\lambda$ becomes large?
o: The policy copies the heart team's treatment for survivors: specificity rises and sensitivity falls
The policy ignores the treatments given, so sensitivity rises
Only deaths are affected, because $G$ is the set of patients who died
The loss reduces to the direct-method estimate of mortality
quiz.e: The penalty is cross-entropy toward the treatment actually given, over survivors $G$. Large $\lambda$ makes the PNN copy the heart team, so survivors' treatments are kept (specificity up) and fewer treatments change overall (sensitivity down). $G$ is the survivors, not the deaths.

quiz.q: How does this study's penalty $\lambda$ parallel ROAD I's weight $\omega$?
o: Both encode prior knowledge: $\omega$ reweights treated patients without recurrence in the counterfactual model, $\lambda$ penalizes changing survivors' treatments in the policy loss; both are tuned by the policy's sensitivity and specificity
Both are weights in the counterfactual model, tuned by cross-validated AUC
$\omega$ penalizes changing treatments in the policy loss, while $\lambda$ reweights treated patients in the outcome model
Both are fixed at 1 before training
quiz.e: ROAD I's prior (imatinib works) enters as $\omega$ on treated patients without recurrence in $h_{t=1}$; here the prior (successful treatments should stand) enters as $\lambda$ in the policy loss. The third option swaps where each enters; neither is tuned by AUC, and $\lambda=1$ was selected by tuning, not fixed.

quiz.q: A policy that never switches any patient's treatment has what specificity and sensitivity?
o: Specificity 1, sensitivity 0
Specificity 0, sensitivity 1
Both 1
Both 0
quiz.e: Specificity is the share of survivors whose treatment is kept (all of them: 1); sensitivity is the share of deaths whose treatment is changed (none: 0). Always switching gives the reverse.

quiz.q: Which cohort may be used to choose $\lambda$?
o: Hartford validation only
Hartford training, where the PNN is fit
St. Vincent's, since it is the most independent
All three cohorts pooled, to maximize sample size
quiz.e: $\lambda$ is a hyperparameter, so it is picked on the validation set. Tuning on training data rewards overfitting, and tuning on St. Vincent's would spend the external test set and bias its estimate.

quiz.q: Why does the LLM only explain the PNN's recommendation instead of choosing the procedure itself?
o: It was not trained on this outcome and is poorly calibrated, and patient records are long and mostly irrelevant
Qwen3-14B cannot process clinical notes
Privacy rules forbid showing LLM output to clinicians
The LLM would first need to be fine-tuned on CT scans
quiz.e: These are the slide's reasons. Privacy decides where the LLM runs (locally, inside the hospital), not whether its text is shown; clinicians do see the explanation, and the LLM reads the record including notes.

quiz.q: In the explanation prompt, what does the LLM do before it reads the PNN's recommendation?
o: Lists the documented findings and judges each one, keeping findings that favor the other procedure
Looks up the patient's 3-year outcome
Drops findings that argue against the recommended procedure
Re-estimates mortality under each procedure
quiz.e: Order: 1 list the documented findings, 2 judge each one, 3 then read the recommendation; findings for the other procedure stay in. Reading the recommendation last keeps the judgments from being bent to fit it, the opposite of the third option.

quiz.q: Why are St. Vincent's rewards computed with reward models frozen after Hartford training, rather than refit on the test cohort as in Lecture 11?
o: St. Vincent's has only 19 SAVR patients (14 deaths), too few to refit the reward models
Refitting would leak test outcomes into the PNN's weights
St. Vincent's records contain no CT scans
Doubly robust rewards cannot be computed on another hospital's data
quiz.e: The slide's reason is size: with about 89% TAVR, the SAVR arm is tiny. The PNN is frozen either way, so refitting reward models would not touch its weights; and held-out DR rewards are computed precisely by applying frozen models to those patients' own outcomes.

quiz.q: Estimated 3-year mortality at St. Vincent's is 11.5% under current practice and 6.4% under the selected policy. Which statement is right?
o: About a 45% relative reduction, from doubly robust estimates whose confidence intervals are wide and include zero
A 5.1-point reduction that is statistically significant
About a 45% relative reduction, confirmed by a randomized trial
About an 80% reduction, matching the policy's specificity
quiz.e: $(11.5-6.4)/11.5\approx0.44$, reported as 45% lower. These are DR estimates from observational data with few deaths, so the intervals include zero; the next step is a pilot at Hartford, not a completed trial.

quiz.q: Blinded cardiologists reviewed 20 Hartford cases: same choice as the model in 10, 'either is fine' in 7, disagree in 3. What share is compatible with the model?
quiz.e: Compatible = same + either is fine = (10+7)/20 = 85% (St. Vincent's: (13+1)/15 = 93%). 50% counts exact agreement only.

written.q: Starting from 597 Hartford training patients with one observed outcome each, explain how the study produces the rewards $\Gamma_{iS},\Gamma_{iT}$ used to train the policy. Formulate the matching step, give the three reward estimators with their weaknesses, explain why matching precedes reweighting and why cross-fitting is used, and state what bias remains.
written.m: Each patient is observed under one procedure only, yet scoring a policy needs estimated 3-year mortality under both, so rewards $\Gamma_{it}$ must be estimated. The data are confounded by risk: in the safest STS bucket 102 of 119 got SAVR, in the riskiest 108 of 121 got TAVR. Matching: score each patient with STS, cut five buckets, and in each bucket solve $\min_z\sum_{i\in S^{min}_k}\sum_{j\in S^{max}_k}z_{ij}\|x_i-x_j\|_2^2$ s.t. $\sum_j z_{ij}=1$ for each $i$ in the smaller arm, $\sum_i z_{ij}\le1$ for each $j$ in the larger arm, $z_{ij}\in\{0,1\}$, with $x$ the standardized (age, sex, BMI). This keeps 326 patients (163 per arm) and drops 271. Rewards: with outcome model $f_t$ (a random survival forest giving P(death within 3 years)) and propensity $p_t$, the direct method $\Gamma_{it}=f_t(x_i)$ is biased if $f_t$ is wrong; IPW $\Gamma_{it}=1\{t_i=t\}y_i/p_t(x_i)$ has high variance when $p_t$ is small; doubly robust $\Gamma_{it}=f_t(x_i)+1\{t_i=t\}(y_i-f_t(x_i))/p_t(x_i)$ is correct if either model is. Matching comes first because before it propensities are extreme (SAVR 13 of 121 in the riskiest bucket, weight about 9; TAVR 17 of 119 in the safest, about 7), making the weights unstable; after matching every bucket is half and half, so weights are about 2. Cross-fitting fits $f_t,p_t$ on four of five folds and computes rewards on the fifth, rotating, so no reward comes from a model trained on that patient. What remains: matching and DR use observed covariates only, so unobserved confounding such as unrecorded frailty (Lecture 14's $U$) can still bias the rewards, and the sample is small with few deaths.
k: One observed outcome per patient; scoring a policy needs both counterfactuals
Confounding by risk, illustrated with bucket counts
Matching: five STS buckets, 1:1 on standardized age, sex, BMI
Correct assignment formulation: =1 for the smaller arm, at most 1 for the larger arm, binary $z$
DM, IPW and DR formulas with failure modes; DR correct if either model is
Matching before reweighting avoids extreme propensities (weights about 9 or 7 fall to about 2)
Cross-fitting: no reward from a model trained on that patient
Residual unobserved confounding and small sample named

written.q: Formulate the prescriptive neural network's training problem, including the cardiologists' penalty. Explain why a softmax is used, what $\lambda$ trades off and how it is chosen, how the selected policy is evaluated out of sample, and how far its results can be trusted.
written.m: The PNN maps embeddings $x_i$ through 64- and 32-unit ReLU layers to scores $s_S,s_T$, with $p_\theta(t\mid x_i)=e^{s_t}/(e^{s_S}+e^{s_T})$. Training solves $\min_\theta\frac1N\sum_i\sum_t p_\theta(t\mid x_i)\Gamma_{it}+\lambda\left(-\frac1{|G|}\sum_{i\in G}\log p_\theta(t_i\mid x_i)\right)$, where $G$ is the survivors and $t_i$ the treatment they received. The first term is expected estimated mortality; it relaxes the Lecture 11 objective $\min_\pi\sum_i\sum_t1\{\pi(x_i)=t\}\Gamma_{it}$, whose hard rule $1\{s_T>s_S\}$ is not differentiable, so the softmax makes it trainable by SGD; the prescription is the larger $p_\theta$. A policy tree was not used because splits on embedding coordinates mean nothing to clinicians. The penalty is cross-entropy toward survivors' treatments ('don't change treatments that already worked'): $\lambda=0$ is the PNN alone, large $\lambda$ copies the heart team, like ROAD I's $\omega$ but placed in the policy loss rather than the counterfactual model. $\lambda$ trades specificity (survivors whose treatment is kept) against sensitivity (deaths whose treatment is changed); larger $\lambda$ raises specificity and lowers sensitivity. It is chosen on Hartford validation only; $\lambda=1$. Evaluation: reward models and PNN are fit on Hartford training and frozen; for held-out patients $\Gamma_{it}$ comes from the frozen reward models and their own outcomes, and $\hat V(\pi)=\frac1n\sum_i\Gamma_{i,\pi(x_i)}$ (St. Vincent's, with 19 SAVR patients, is too small to refit). Results: estimated mortality 7.0% to 4.7% at Hartford (34% lower) and 11.5% to 6.4% at St. Vincent's (45% lower); specificity 0.80 and 0.79, sensitivity 0.50 at both; blinded cardiologists judged 85% and 93% of choices compatible. Trust is limited: these are DR estimates from observational data with few deaths, the intervals are wide and include zero, unobserved confounding may remain, and only death within 3 years is counted, hence the planned pilot at Hartford HealthCare.
k: Softmax policy definition and network shape
Full loss: expected estimated mortality plus $\lambda$ cross-entropy over survivors
Why softmax: differentiable relaxation of the hard rule, trainable by SGD
Why not a policy tree: splits on embeddings are uninterpretable
Meaning of $\lambda$ (0 = PNN alone, large = copy heart team) and the $\omega$ analogy
Sensitivity and specificity defined; direction of the $\lambda$ trade-off; chosen on Hartford validation ($\lambda=1$)
Off-policy evaluation with frozen reward models and $\hat V(\pi)$
Caveats: CIs include zero, unobserved confounding, single outcome, need for a pilot
